summary: Describes an operational technique that uses BGP communities to remotely trigger black-holing of a destination network, in order to block denial-of-service attacks. The black-holing can be applied on selected routers. It also describes a sinkhole tunnel approach.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3882 describes how an operator can use Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) route tags to block attack traffic at selected routers. It also describes sending traffic through a tunnel to a router for inspection.

questions: how to block ddos with bgp
how does bgp community blackholing work
how can an operator target selected routers
subtitle: Using BGP communities to direct selected routers to discard traffic under attack.

tldr.problem: A denial-of-service attack can send unwanted traffic toward a network. A network-wide black-hole route can stop the traffic but may also make the targeted network unreachable through the whole autonomous system.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3882 describes tagging an attacked route with BGP communities so only selected border routers change its next hop to a null interface; it also describes redirecting traffic through a sinkhole tunnel for analysis.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents an operational technique, not a new BGP protocol. Its route policies must prevent external peers from using the special community to black-hole arbitrary routes.

facts.label: Target route recommendation
facts.value: Black-hole targeted hosts rather than the whole address block

today: RFC 3882 is an Informational document describing an operational BGP configuration technique. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Earlier Black-Hole Approach
sections.content:
In the approach described in section 1, an operator changes the BGP next hop for an attacked prefix across the destination autonomous system. Routers configured to send a private next-hop address to a null interface then discard traffic for that route.

This can shield internal infrastructure, but it also makes the target unreachable throughout the autonomous system, including to legitimate users. The document describes this limitation as the reason for selecting routers rather than applying the change everywhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A network-wide black-hole route can stop unwanted traffic by discarding packets for a target. It also blocks legitimate traffic to that target across the network.

sections.title: Targeting Routers with Communities
sections.content:
The enhanced technique assigns BGP community values to identify individual border routers or a set of routers. During an attack, the operator announces the target prefix with the community for the routers where the attack enters. Only routers configured to match that community change the route's next hop to a null interface.

The route policy also matches locally generated advertisements, so an external BGP peer cannot use the community to make the network discard traffic for an arbitrary prefix. The RFC recommends targeting host routes where possible to limit the effect on the attacked network.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP route tag can tell selected border routers to discard traffic for a target. The routing rule must also check that the instruction came from inside the operator's network.

sections.title: Using a Sinkhole Tunnel for Analysis
sections.content:
Instead of discarding traffic immediately, an operator can direct it through a tunnel to a sinkhole router with an attached traffic-analysis device. The border routers selected by the community send matching traffic into the tunnel; other routers continue normal routing.

The sinkhole can inspect traffic and may forward it toward its destination afterward. The RFC cautions that diverting a prefix to a sinkhole can interrupt service if legitimate traffic is captured and not forwarded. It describes MPLS Traffic Engineering as one example of a way to build the tunnel.
sections.plainLanguage: A special tunnel sends selected traffic to a router where it can be inspected. If legitimate packets are captured and not forwarded, the destination's service is still interrupted.

sections.title: Protecting the Route Policy
sections.content:
The RFC stresses that external BGP peers must not be allowed to trigger black-holing for arbitrary networks. The special route policy should match both the selected community and an AS path showing that the advertised prefix was generated locally.

Operators need tight control over external BGP peering before using this technique. Without the local-route check, an external peer could attach a special community to a route and cause traffic to that route to be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: The network must verify that a black-hole instruction applies to a route it generated itself. Otherwise, an external peer could try to make the network discard traffic to an unrelated destination.
